title: Data from Configuration Repository: SNMP (MIB Dump)
shortTitle: Data from Configuration Repository: SNMP (MIB Dump)
summary: SNMP MIB Dump is the sub-technique of Data from Configuration Repository in which the adversary reads the Management Information Base of network devices over Simple Network Management Protocol. The Management Information Base is a structured repository: every manageable variable has an object identifier, a numeric address in a tree, and holds values such as the system description, hardware model, physical location, installed software, interface counters, address resolution entries, routing information and parts of the running configuration. Reading is a first class function of the protocol, so an adversary with a valid community string or user credentials can walk the tree and retrieve the whole dataset without changing anything on the device. Bulk retrieval operations make this both fast and quiet, and the collected output feeds network mapping, target selection and later exploitation. Because the traffic is normal management protocol, content inspection is of limited value; the tell is behaviour. Legitimate management comes from a small number of known hosts, on a schedule, using specific object identifiers or narrow ranges, often with read only credentials. Adversarial walks come from unexpected sources, at odd hours, traverse large parts of the tree in one session, repeat across many devices in sequence, and may use default or vendor shipped community strings. Monitoring device query logs, management platform authentication records and flow data for the source and volume of management traffic is what separates the two.

beginner.definition: Simple Network Management Protocol, usually shortened to SNMP, is a common way to monitor network devices. A Management Information Base, or MIB, is the list of values those devices can report. This sub-technique describes an attacker reading that whole list.
beginner.whyItMatters: The MIB can reveal device models, software versions, locations and network routes. That is exactly what an attacker needs to choose targets. Reading it changes nothing, so the device raises no fault and users see no outage. Only careful logging of management traffic shows that a stranger asked for everything.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains a community string or user account for SNMP on the device.
They send normal read requests for many object identifiers in a row.
Each object identifier points to one stored value in the device tree.
They walk the tree and collect system, interface, routing and address details.
They repeat this across many devices to build a picture of the network.
They then use that map to plan which systems to attack next.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse where every shelf has a code, and a printed list shows what sits on each shelf. Staff use that list to find goods quickly. A stranger with a visitor badge can stand in the aisle and copy the entire list onto his phone. The shelves are untouched and the stock is complete, so no alarm sounds. Yet the stranger now knows where the expensive items are and when the spare keys are stored. Walking the Management Information Base works like copying that list. The attacker takes no goods, but leaves with a perfect map of the building.
takeaways: Treat SNMP as a data source that needs both strong credentials and tight access control.
Alert on bulk queries from hosts that do not normally manage the network.
Retire default community strings and prefer the modern authenticated version of the protocol.

objectives: Explain what a Management Information Base is and how object identifiers address it.
Describe how an adversary walks an SNMP tree to collect device and network data.
State how this sub-technique differs from a full configuration file export.
Identify the log and flow data that reveals unusual SNMP querying.
Compare legitimate monitoring polls with a bulk information gathering session.
Explain how collected data supports later network mapping.
